Most ecosystems have complex feeding links.
Changes to one species can affect others.
How can camouflage help both predators and prey?
Prey can hide from hunters, and hunters can sneak closer to prey.
Camouflage removes the need for any food.
Camouflage turns animals into plants permanently.
Camouflage only works on animals that live in space.
Blending into surroundings is useful on both sides of a hunt. Color, pattern, and shape can all contribute.
Camouflage is a common adaptation.
Survival strategies differ by species and habitat.
How do most mammal babies begin life compared with many insects?
Most mammals are born live and are fed milk by a parent.
Most mammals hatch as caterpillars first.
Most mammals start as seeds in soil.
Most mammals never need parental care.
Mammal life cycles usually include live birth and milk feeding. Insect life cycles often include very different looking stages.
Life cycles vary across animal groups.
Parental care is common in mammals.
Why do many birds build nests?
Nests give eggs and chicks a safer place to develop.
Nests are used to store sunlight for winter.
Nests replace a bird's need to eat.
Nests turn eggs into mammals.
A nest holds eggs and shelters chicks. Location and materials vary by bird species.
Animal homes support reproduction and survival.
Disturbing nests can harm young birds.
If predators disappear from an ecosystem, what might happen?
Some prey populations may grow too large and harm plants or balance.
Nothing in the ecosystem would ever change.
Plants would stop needing sunlight.
Prey would instantly become producers.
Predators help regulate prey numbers. Without them, overgrazing or other imbalances can follow.
Ecosystem roles are connected.
Balance depends on many species, not one alone.
Which set lists basic needs of most plants?
Light, water, air, and nutrients
Homework, Wi-Fi, and headphones
Only darkness and motor oil
Only plastic and salt crystals
Plants use light energy and take in water, air, and nutrients to live and grow. Missing needs limit growth.
Living things have requirements for survival.
Garden care matches plant needs.
Why are leaves especially important for a plant?
Capture light and help make food for the plant
Chase insects across the ground
Pump blood to animal hearts
Store electricity for cities
Most photosynthesis happens in leaves. That food energy supports roots, stems, flowers, and fruits.
Leaf shape and arrangement can affect light capture.
Green plants rely on leaf function.
How do roots growing into soil mainly help a plant?
Anchoring it and taking up water and minerals
Flying it to new gardens
Making nectar for its own stomach
Hearing sounds underground
Anchoring prevents tipping. Absorption supplies materials the plant needs for growth and photosynthesis.
Root systems can be shallow or deep.
Soil quality affects root health.
What is the main job of flowers on many plants?
Reproduction—helping the plant make seeds
Digesting rocks into soil vitamins
Pumping sap like an animal heart
Scaring away all sunlight
Flowers contain reproductive parts. After pollination and fertilization, seeds (often inside fruits) can form.
Flowers are key to many plant life cycles.
Pollinators often assist flowering plants.
Where does digestion of food begin?
In the mouth, where chewing and saliva start breaking food down
Only in the hair follicles
Only in the fingernails
Only in the outer ear
Teeth grind food and saliva begins chemical breakdown. Digestion continues in the stomach and intestines.
Mechanical and chemical digestion work together.
The digestive tract is a long pathway for food.
What is the main job of the lungs?
Exchange gases—taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide
Store undigested bones
Produce pollen for plants
Pump blood instead of the heart
Air enters the lungs, where oxygen moves into blood and carbon dioxide moves out to be exhaled.
Breathing supports cellular energy needs.
Lung health matters for activity and life.
Why are teeth important for digestion?
They break food into smaller pieces that are easier to swallow and digest.
They filter wastes from the blood like kidneys.
They carry nerve signals to the toes only.
They produce red blood cells.
Chewing increases food's surface area so enzymes can work better. Different teeth shapes suit cutting and grinding.
Dental care supports good nutrition.
Digestion is harder with very large unchewed bites.
What is the main job of the heart?
Pump blood through the circulatory system
Make bile for plant roots
Store memories in bone marrow only
Digest proteins in the mouth
Each heartbeat pushes blood into vessels. Circulation delivers oxygen and nutrients and removes wastes.
Heart muscle works continuously.
Exercise can strengthen cardiovascular fitness.
If your pulse is faster, what is usually true?
Your heart is beating more times per minute.
Your bones have disappeared.
Your skin has stopped sensing touch.
Your stomach has become a lung.
Pulse rate matches heart rate. Exercise, excitement, or fever can raise how often the heart beats.
You can measure pulse at wrist or neck.
Resting rates are usually lower than exercise rates.
How does oxygen from the air reach body cells?
Lungs put oxygen into blood, and blood carries it to cells.
Oxygen travels only through hair strands.
Oxygen is digested in the large intestine first.
Oxygen reaches cells only through the skin's sweat glands.
Gas exchange in the lungs loads red blood cells with oxygen. Circulation then delivers that oxygen throughout the body.
Respiratory and circulatory systems work together.
Cells use oxygen to release energy from nutrients.
Why does blood flow to muscles increase during exercise?
Active muscles need more oxygen and nutrients delivered quickly.
Muscles stop using energy during exercise.
Blood flow increases to turn muscles into fat instantly.
Exercise shuts down the heart's pumping.
Working muscles have higher demand. The body responds by sending more blood where it is needed most.
Circulation adjusts to activity level.
Breathing rate often rises along with heart rate.
What happens when you touch something hot?
Nerves quickly send danger signals so you can pull away.
Your bones dissolve to cool the object.
Your hair digests the heat.
Your lungs store the heat as sugar.
Sensory nerves detect heat and pain. The nervous system triggers a fast response to protect you from burns.
Reflexes can act very quickly.
Nerves link sensors, spinal cord, and brain.
How do kidneys mainly help keep the body in balance?
Removing wastes and extra water from the blood
Producing oxygen for photosynthesis
Chewing food before it reaches the mouth
Replacing the brain during sleep
Filtering blood protects the internal environment. Urine carries removed wastes out of the body.
Excretory organs manage wastes.
Blood composition stays within healthy ranges partly thanks to kidneys.
What can skipping a warm-up before intense activity increase the chance of?
Muscle strains and other injuries
Instant photosynthesis in skin
Growing a second skeleton overnight
Never needing water again
Cold, tight muscles and sudden hard effort raise injury risk. Warming up prepares tissues for stress.
Preparation supports safe performance.
Cool-downs after exercise also help recovery.
What should a good hypothesis be?
A clear, testable prediction based on what you know
A secret answer you refuse to check
A random doodle unrelated to the question
A final grade for the experiment before testing
Good hypotheses guide what to measure. Experiments then produce evidence about the prediction.
Testable ideas drive investigations.
Revise thinking when evidence disagrees.
What belongs in a data table during an experiment?
Organized measurements and observations from each trial
Only jokes with no numbers
Only the title of your favorite movie
Only guesses with no recording of results
Tables capture what happened in a structured way. Labels, units, and trial numbers keep data usable.
Good records support analysis.
Others should be able to read your table.
Which tool measures length most directly?
A ruler or meter stick
A stopwatch only
A balance scale only
Rulers measure distance or length. Other tools measure different quantities like time, mass, or temperature.
Read the scale carefully at eye level.
In an experiment on fertilizer and plant height, what is the fertilizer amount usually called?
Independent variable (what you change)
Unit of temperature
Safety goggle type
Title of the graph only
You change fertilizer levels on purpose. Plant height would be what you measure as a possible effect.
Independent variable: what you change.
Dependent variable: what you measure.
Which is a basic science-class safety rule?
Follow teacher directions and wear required protective gear.
Run with glassware for speed trials.
Taste unknown powders to identify them.
Remove labels from chemical bottles for fun.
Rules and protective gear prevent injuries. Listening carefully keeps everyone safer during investigations.
Safety is part of scientific practice.
Tell a teacher about spills or accidents right away.
Why is a control setup useful in an experiment?
Shows what happens without the experimental change
Lets you skip measuring the test group
Proves every hypothesis true automatically
Removes units from all data
Without a control, it is harder to know whether your change mattered. The control is the comparison baseline.
Fair tests need thoughtful comparisons.
Keep non-tested conditions the same.
Why do scientists often repeat the same trial many times?
To build confidence that results are not just a one-time accident
To ignore safety rules
To change two variables secretly
To avoid writing units
Repeats reveal consistency. Outliers become clearer, and average trends are more trustworthy.
Reliability grows with careful repetition.
Report all honest trials, not only favorites.
